name: たけだの穴子めし まねき本店 (Takeda no Anago-meshi Maneki Honten)

claims.text: No allergen disclosure is published. The cooking liquid and sauce contain standard Japanese soy sauce (wheat). Cross-contamination risk within the bento kitchen is unknown.

The proprietary tare used to glaze and simmer the anago is made with soy sauce; Japanese soy sauce (koikuchi) standardly contains wheat. The rice is cooked in the same anago-shoyu dashi. No GF soy sauce alternative is mentioned anywhere.
The entire product is animal-based (eel, eel dashi, shoyu). There is no plant-based item on the menu and no segregation relevant to vegan contact.
No published allergy protocol. Reservations are available and phone inquiries are possible (079-223-8652), but no allergy accommodation policy has been documented.
Simple, focused menu of just two bento sizes means ingredient consistency is high — what you get today is what every other customer gets.

No information on cross-contamination controls is available from any source reviewed. The small open-counter kitchen format means multiple courses with wheat-containing ingredients are prepared in the same space.

Traditional Japanese kaiseki at this level standardly uses wheat-containing koikuchi shoyu and mirin throughout — in marinades, glazes, and sauces. No tamari or GF soy sauce alternative is mentioned anywhere.
Dashi is the foundational liquid in kaiseki cuisine; at this restaurant it is almost certainly fish-based (katsuo/konbu). No plant-based dashi alternative is listed or implied by any reviewed source.

No allergy-handling protocol or staff allergen training is documented on any platform. Phone reservations are standard and the restaurant explicitly recommends calling ahead to discuss meal preparation — this is the appropriate channel to raise dietary needs.
12-seat intimate format with an owner-chef who cooks every course means direct dialogue about dietary needs is possible when flagged well in advance by phone.

The kitchen prepares yakisoba (wheat noodles) alongside oden and grilled items in what is currently a compact temporary outdoor setup, making cross-contamination a realistic concern. No separation protocols have been documented.

Himeji oden is defined by its ginger soy sauce finish (生姜醤油). Standard Japanese soy sauce (shoyu) contains wheat as a primary ingredient. The oden broth itself is soy-sauce-based, so gluten is embedded in the dish's identity, not just a condiment.
The entire menu is built around chicken and dashi-based broth. There is no plant-based cooking line and no documented effort to keep any item free of animal products.

No allergy-handling protocols or English-language allergy communication have been documented for this restaurant. The staff environment is Japanese-only and the kitchen is a temporary setup post-fire.
The restaurant accepts credit cards (JCB, AMEX, Diners) and PayPay, reducing one barrier for foreign visitors, and single diners are explicitly welcome at the counter.

name: 天ぷらと小鉢料理 だん乃 (Tempura to Kobachi Ryori Danno)

claims.text: All tempura — seafood and vegetable alike — is fried in the same oil at an open counter. No dedicated GF fryer is mentioned in any source.
No wheat-free soy sauce (tamari) is mentioned. Standard Japanese soy sauce, which contains wheat, is the baseline ingredient across sauces, dipping broths, and oden broth.
Vegetable tempura shares fryer oil with shrimp, fish, and other seafood items cooked to order in the same vessel at the counter.
Open counter seating lets diners see exactly what is being fried and in what order, which at least allows direct conversation with the chef about specific requests.
High-volume standing counter with multiple fish preparations happening simultaneously; no separation of GF and non-GF prep surfaces documented.
Standard Japanese soy sauce is used on nigiri at the counter; no GF soy sauce (tamari) or wheat-free shoyu option has been mentioned in any review or listing.
The entire menu is seafood-based; no plant-only preparation zones exist. Miso soup served with sets contains fish-based dashi.
No allergy handling procedures, dedicated allergen menu, or staff allergy training have been documented in any source reviewed.
Rice (shari) itself uses only Kinuhikari rice and a vinegar blend — the rice base is wheat-free, which is the foundation of each nigiri.
Standard izakaya kitchen with no GF segregation advertised. Wheat-based soy sauce and dashi are core to virtually every dish. Cross-contamination risk is high.

Traditional Japanese soy sauce (含む小麦) is the backbone of Japanese izakaya cooking and almost certainly used throughout the menu — in marinades, tare, dipping sauces, and oden broth. No wheat-free shoyu or tamari alternatives are mentioned.
Bonito-based (katsuobushi) dashi is standard in Japanese izakaya broth, sauces, and oden. Seafood is central to the menu concept. No plant-based preparation stream exists.
No allergen menu, allergy handling protocol, or foreign-language dietary communication noted on any source. Direct inquiry by phone in Japanese is the only confirmed route.
Cards widely accepted (Visa, MC, Amex, JCB, Diners, e-money); counter seating available for solo diners; reservations accepted by phone and online.
No published information on cross-contamination controls. Fried items (scorpionfish karaage) appear on menus, indicating shared frying oil with wheat-battered foods is possible.

Traditional kappo cooking uses wheat-containing soy sauce throughout — in dipping sauces, simmered dishes, and marinades. No tamari or gluten-free soy sauce alternative is mentioned anywhere in available sources.
All courses are built around fish and seafood; bonito/katsuo dashi is standard in Japanese kappo cooking. No vegan-safe preparation lines are indicated.
No information on allergy handling procedures is publicly available. Diners with celiac disease or serious allergies should call the restaurant directly (079-288-0878) well before visiting.

name: ベジタブルカフェ さくらさく (Vegetable Cafe Sakura Saku)

claims.text: The dessert menu includes handmade vegetable chiffon cake made with domestic wheat flour; wheat is actively used in the kitchen and cross-contamination of shared prep surfaces must be assumed.
Soy sauce is used in cooking (confirmed in tofu steak soy-ginger glaze); standard Japanese shoyu contains wheat. Tamari substitution has not been documented for this restaurant.

The daily lunch includes a meat or fish main course prepared in the same kitchen as the vegetable sides; those requesting a fully vegan meal should specify clearly when ordering so the kitchen can plate separately.

Staff are noted for consulting individually with each customer about dietary preferences and restrictions — including international guests — and can adapt the meal composition accordingly. Phone ahead (079-222-1220) is recommended for specific allergy needs.

All stocks (dashi) are made exclusively from shiitake mushroom and konbu kelp — no katsuobushi, saba-bushi, or other animal-derived ingredients — making the flavour base inherently vegan and free from a common hidden-allergen risk.
The kitchen avoids chemical additives entirely, using only natural, whole-food ingredients sourced from the family's wholesale produce connections.
